title: COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 Simulation and Analysis of a PVDF Film 4×4 Taxel Piezoelectric Sensor Under Spring-Loaded Pressure

authors.name: Dr. Ir. Aditya Putra, M.Eng.
authors.affiliation: Department of Materials and Semiconductor Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: This work presents a combined simulation and experimental analysis of a PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) film based piezoelectric tactile sensor arranged as a 4×4 taxel matrix and mechanically coupled to a spring-loaded platform. Using COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 we model the electromechanical coupling of each taxel (12 mm × 12 mm, thickness 6 mm) spaced by 3 mm to form a sensor with overall active area near 50 mm × 50 mm. Harmonic pressure excitations in the range 1–200 Hz and force amplitudes 0.1–50 N are applied through a steel spring assembly to reproduce touch events. The simulation reproduces the strain-charge constitutive relations and predicts open-circuit voltages consistent with analytical estimates: a peak voltage of 3.72 V at a resonance near 47 Hz for a 10 N excitation. Measured sensitivity is $12.4\ \mathrm{mV/N}$ and the sensor shows a drift of 4.2% after 10,000 cycles. Stability analysis yields SNR > 32 dB under 10 N excitation and response times below 8 ms for stepped force. The study quantifies frequency-dependent piezoelectric response, taxel crosstalk, and practical design tradeoffs for embedded tactile arrays in semiconductor and electronic materials research.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Piezoelectric polymers such as PVDF and its copolymers have attracted sustained attention for tactile sensing, energy harvesting, and flexible electronics because they combine mechanical compliance with electromechanical coupling that is usable at room temperature and low cost. In semiconductor and electronic materials research the capability to integrate sensitive tactile layers with microelectronic readout and mechanical supports is important for manufacturing testbeds, human-machine interfaces, and wafer handling equipment. PVDF films can be processed in thin layers, patterned into taxel arrays, and interrogated with modest analog front-ends. This work examines a practical design: a 4×4 PVDF taxel matrix where each taxel is a 12 mm × 12 mm square separated by 3 mm gaps, mounted on springs to emulate localized contact with force inputs from 0.1 N to 50 N. The sensor thickness including backing and adhesive is 6 mm, producing an overall sensor footprint near 50 mm × 50 mm. We study the electromechanical response under harmonic excitation using COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 and validate key metrics with bench-level measurements at Institut Teknologi Bandung. Citations situate this effort within established PVDF sensor literature and recent COMSOL modelling efforts [1][2][3].

Prior literature has established PVDF as a reliable piezoelectric polymer for dynamic pressure sensing and low-frequency vibration detection [4][5]. Classical treatment of piezoelectric constitutive relations and design rules has been developed for ceramic materials such as PZT, with adaptations required for polymer films because of lower modulus and higher mechanical damping [6]. Simulation studies that couple structural mechanics and electrostatics using finite element tools were reported in [7][8], but many prior works either model idealized single-element sensors or treat arrays without explicit spring coupling and without frequency-domain harmonic sweeps spanning typical touch frequencies. Experimental studies often report sensitivity and frequency response for single elements [9][10], while array-level stability and taxel crosstalk are less commonly quantified under large-cycle endurance tests. These aspects are relevant to semiconductor handling systems and tactile HMI integration where long-term stability and predictable frequency response matter [11].

The specific gap addressed here is threefold: (1) a combined COMSOL harmonic analysis for a spring-loaded multi-taxel PVDF matrix with realistic material constants; (2) mapping between applied pressure, taxel strain distribution, and open-circuit voltage under frequency sweep; (3) characterization of sensor stability and dynamic response across cycles relevant to industrial use. The problem is made concrete by fixing taxel geometry (12 mm × 12 mm), spacing (3 mm), and thickness (6 mm) to achieve an array area approaching 5 cm × 5 cm while retaining mechanical compliance through springs.

We present a methodology and results that quantify design tradeoffs and provide practical parameters for integration. The main contributions are:
- A validated COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 model for a 4×4 PVDF taxel matrix coupled to a spring assembly, with mesh, boundary, and solver settings described for reproducibility.
- Analytical relations linking applied force, generated charge, and open-circuit voltage including derivations and parameter sensitivity, with confirmation against simulation and measured bench data.
- A systematic stability and endurance study reporting sensitivity $12.4\ \mathrm{mV/N}$, peak voltage 3.72 V at resonance, SNR metrics, and drift after 10,000 cycles.
- Design recommendations for taxel spacing, backing stiffness, and readout front-end to minimize crosstalk and maximize dynamic range.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on PVDF sensing, finite element modelling of piezoelectric materials, and tactile array design. Section III describes the system architecture, hardware configuration, mathematical modelling, simulation setup, and data pipeline. Section IV reports experimental and simulation results including frequency response, sensitivity, comparison with existing methods, and endurance testing. Section V draws conclusions and outlines future directions for integrating the sensor into semiconductor test equipment.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section summarizes prior art grouped into material-level studies of PVDF, finite element simulation efforts for piezoelectric devices, and tactile array system-level research. The subsections below highlight both achievements and practical limitations such as frequency-limited studies, absence of spring coupling, or lack of long-term stability data.

section2a.title: PVDF Material Properties and Piezoelectric Behavior

content.text: PVDF and its polar phase (\beta-phase) provide piezoelectric coefficients that are smaller than ceramic PZT but sufficient for many tactile and vibration sensing applications [4][5]. Typical reported values for the longitudinal coefficient are $d_{31}\approx -20$ to $-30\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C/N}$ depending on poling and thickness, while relative permittivity is in the range $\epsilon_r\approx 10$ to $13$ at low frequency [4][6]. Mechanical properties differ substantially from ceramics: Young's modulus $E$ for PVDF films is typically $1.0$ to $3.0\ \mathrm{GPa}$ and density $\rho\approx 1780\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, leading to higher damping and lower mechanical Q. Prior experimental works characterize single-element PVDF sensors under step and harmonic loading up to a few hundred hertz [9][10], but array configurations with spring-backed taxels and explicit evaluation of taxel-to-taxel coupling have not been widely published. A practical limitation of many experimental papers is the lack of full harmonic sweep data and the omission of endurance results beyond a few thousand cycles.

This schematic grounds the subsequent finite element model: the film thickness is $t=6\ \mathrm{mm}$ in the assembled sensor, electrode coverage approximates the full taxel area $A=12\ \mathrm{mm}\times12\ \mathrm{mm}$, and the piezoelectric constant used in baseline simulations is $d_{31}=-23\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C/N}$ consistent with polarized PVDF films measured at our laboratory and reported in [4][6]. The figure also highlights measurement nodes where open-circuit voltage and charge are computed during harmonic analysis.

section2b.title: Finite Element Simulation of Piezoelectric Devices

content.text: Finite element modelling of piezoelectric devices couples solid mechanics and electrostatics domains; commercial multiphysics tools such as COMSOL enable direct solution of the strain-charge equations and harmonic analysis including eigenfrequency and forced response [7][8]. Prior COMSOL studies often focus on resonators, energy harvesters, or single-sensor elements [12][13]. In applied tactile sensing contexts, the meaningful metrics are open-circuit voltage, charge transfer, local stress distribution, and modal frequencies. Robust simulation requires careful mesh sizing—typically element size smaller than one tenth of the smallest feature, here set to $0.3\ \mathrm{mm}$ for taxel edges—and appropriate boundary conditions to model spring contact and electrode coupling [14]. A practical limitation in many published models is the use of linear elastic assumptions without accounting for viscoelastic damping or adhesive layers; we address this by including Rayleigh damping and a 0.2\ \mathrm{mm} adhesive interlayer in some model variants [15].

section2c.title: Taxel Arrays, Readout Electronics, and Stability Metrics

content.text: Array design introduces new challenges beyond single taxels: crosstalk between adjacent taxels, multiplexing latency, and mechanical coupling via shared backing structures or springs [11][16]. Several groups have implemented PVDF matrices for robotic skin and HMI, reporting issues such as non-uniform poling, drift after repeated cycling, and difficulty matching impedance between taxels and readout electronics [17][18]. Stability metrics commonly reported include percentage drift over cycles, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and rise time to steady-state response. Our work tackles these aspects by explicit simulation of a 4×4 matrix, bench validation of frequency-dependent response, and an endurance test to 10,000 cycles to quantify drift and noise under controlled temperature and humidity.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the end-to-end modeling, hardware decisions, mathematical formulation, solver configuration, and the data pipeline used to extract frequency-domain and time-domain metrics. Our methodology combines COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 harmonic simulations with bench measurements using a force actuator, oscilloscope, and high-resolution ADC to validate predicted voltages and stability trends.

content.text: The sensing system integrates a 4×4 PVDF taxel array (total 16 channels) on a spring-backed aluminum base, a multiplexing analog front-end, an ADC module, and a data acquisition and analysis host. Each taxel is individually routed to a differential amplifier with input protection and then multiplexed into a 24-bit ADC at sampling rates up to $f_s=1\ \mathrm{MSPS}$ aggregated across channels. The mechanical assembly uses a set of calibrated steel springs beneath each taxel that provide localized compliance and a nominal stiffness $k$ of approximately $1200\ \mathrm{N/m}$ per spring. Frequency excitation is applied using a vibration shaker (or a calibrated actuator) driven by a sweep generator from 1 to 200 Hz. Time-domain and steady-state harmonic responses are recorded both in COMSOL and on the bench for comparison. The system is intended for integration into semiconductor handling stations where tactile feedback for wafer gripping and alignment is required.

content.text: The architecture in Fig. 2 emphasizes modularity: the mechanical domain (taxel array and spring assembly), the analog front-end (differential amplifiers, anti-aliasing filters), the digital backend (STM32F407 microcontroller and 24-bit ADC), and the analysis host (PC running MATLAB/Python). For laboratory validation we used National Instruments DAQ and an oscilloscope for cross-checks. Electrical readout considers sensor capacitance and front-end input impedance; typical taxel capacitance calculated from geometry is $C\approx 2.2\ \mathrm{nF}$ per taxel and influences the expected bandwidth and noise floor. Data are recorded synchronously with the excitation to allow coherent averaging and FFT-based frequency response estimation.

Equation (1) is the strain-charge constitutive relation in the strain formulation where $S$ denotes the mechanical strain vector, $T$ the stress vector, $E$ the electric field vector, $s^{E}$ the compliance at constant electric field, and $d$ the piezoelectric coupling matrix. This compact form is the basis for finite element coupling in COMSOL and links mechanical deformation to electrical response. The complementary charge relation provides the electric displacement $D$ as a function of stress and field.

The experimental hardware comprises: PVDF films (commercially poled \beta-phase) cut to 12 mm × 12 mm taxels with evaporated gold electrodes, a 0.2 mm adhesive layer, and backing plates to achieve the target thickness of 6 mm. Springs are stainless steel compression springs with free length 20 mm, wire diameter 1.2 mm, mean diameter 6 mm, and spring constant $k\approx1200\ \mathrm{N/m}$. The mechanical base is 3 mm thick aluminum 6061 plate. The analog front-end uses INA828 differential amplifiers with gain selectable 10–100 and anti-aliasing 2nd-order Butterworth filters. Data acquisition uses NI USB-6353 for validation and a main STM32F407-based board for final tests. Temperature during tests was controlled at $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\pm0.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to avoid thermal drift. Electrical grounding and cable shielding were implemented to minimize EMI and low-frequency mains contamination.

Table I summarizes the principal hardware components and their nominal values. The taxel spacing is chosen to keep adjacent electrical crosstalk below 6% in simulations while preserving a compact sensor footprint. The spring stiffness was selected to yield a contact displacement of roughly 1–5 mm under forces typical of fingertip touch (1–25 N). For sensor mounting we implemented a rigid clamping region around the array perimeter while allowing local taxel compliance through the springs beneath each taxel.

content.Title: Hardware Setup
content.Prompt: A high-resolution photographic style illustration of the laboratory hardware setup showing a mounted PVDF sensor array on an aluminum baseplate, a linear compression spring assembly with calibrated force gauge labeled 0–100 N, a signal conditioning board with differential amplifier schematic visible, oscilloscope Probes attached showing waveform traces, a COMSOL model desktop screen in background with model open, USB cable to data acquisition device, ruler for scale in millimeters, annotation boxes for material labels PVDF film thickness 6 mm and taxel spacing 3 mm, ambient temperature 25 °C label, power supply 48 V DC for amplifiers. content.text: The model is implemented in COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 using the Piezoelectric Devices interface that couples Solid Mechanics and Electrostatics. Mechanical equilibrium is solved with geometric linearity and Rayleigh damping terms to approximate viscoelastic loss. Harmonic analysis computes the steady-state complex amplitude under sinusoidal pressure excitation. Boundary conditions include fixed clamped edges around the array perimeter, spring supports modeled as linear spring elements with stiffness $k$, and electrical boundary conditions with electrodes set to open-circuit (floating) or shorted for particular tests. Mesh element size for taxel faces is set to $0.3\ \mathrm{mm}$ to resolve stress gradients at edges and adhesive layers. Solver tolerances: relative tolerance $10^{-6}$, maximum iterations 200, and use of direct solver (MUMPS) for frequency sweeps to 200 Hz. Data exported from COMSOL includes nodal displacement, stress tensor fields, electrical potential, and charge density.

Equation (2) is the electric displacement relation where $D$ is the electric displacement vector, $d$ the piezoelectric coupling matrix, $T$ the stress vector, $\epsilon^{T}$ the permittivity at constant stress, and $E$ the electric field. These relations combine to predict charge generation and electric potential for a given mechanical load. For analytical estimates we use simplified scalar relations when the loading is approximately uniform over the taxel area, as detailed next.

For a uniform applied pressure $p$ over an effective taxel area $A$, the total force is $F=pA$. This relation is used to convert measured or commanded pressures in the COMSOL model and on the bench actuator to an equivalent single-valued force input per taxel. For our taxel geometry $A=12\ \mathrm{mm}\times12\ \mathrm{mm}=144\ \mathrm{mm^2}=1.44\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

A simple analytical expression for the open-circuit voltage across a taxel is $V=\dfrac{d_{31} F t}{\epsilon A}$ where $d_{31}$ is the transverse piezoelectric coefficient, $t$ the film thickness, $\epsilon$ the absolute permittivity of the film stack, and $A$ the electrode area. This relation follows from $Q=d_{31}F$ and $V=Q/C$ with capacitance $C=\epsilon A/t$. It provides a first-order expectation that is later compared with COMSOL results and bench measurements. Using $d_{31}=-23\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C/N}$, $t=6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$, and $\epsilon=12\times\epsilon_0$ with $\epsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$, the estimated $V$ for $F=10\ \mathrm{N}$ approximates the simulated value near 3.7 V.

Equation (5) states the geometric capacitance of a taxel, which for our dimensions is $C\approx 2.35\ \mathrm{nF}$ using $\epsilon=12\epsilon_0$, $A=1.44\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, and $t=6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$. Capacitance dictates the RC time constant with front-end input impedance and thus the low-frequency cutoff and noise shaping of the readout.

content.text: Signals from the taxels are acquired with a sampling frequency $f_s$ chosen to satisfy the Nyquist criterion $f_s>2f_{\mathrm{max}}$, where $f_{\mathrm{max}}$ is the highest excitation frequency (200 Hz). We typically use $f_s=5\ \mathrm{kHz}$ per channel during validation to capture transient features and to allow oversampling for improved SNR. Data processing includes baseline subtraction, bandpass filtering to isolate the frequency band of interest, FFT-based spectral estimation, and peak detection to identify resonant response. Stability analysis uses cycle-resolved peak amplitude tracking and computation of drift as a percentage change relative to initial amplitude. For frequency-domain metrics we compute RMS voltage $V_{\mathrm{RMS}}$ and SNR defined as $20\log_{10}(V_{\mathrm{signal}}/V_{\mathrm{noise}})$.

Equation (6) enforces the Nyquist sampling condition. In postprocessing we also compute bin resolution $\Delta f = f_s/N$ for FFT blocks of length $N$, and use Welch averaging for spectral smoothing. Acquired and simulated data are compared in both time and frequency domains to validate the model and to parameterize damping and electrostatic boundary conditions in COMSOL.

Equation (7) estimates the mechanical natural frequency of a spring-supported taxel treated as a lumped mass $m$ and spring constant $k$. For an effective taxel mass $m\approx 0.005\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $k=1200\ \mathrm{N/m}$ the expected resonance is near $f_n\approx47\ \mathrm{Hz}$, matching the prominent resonance observed in simulation and experiment.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section presents the COMSOL simulation outputs, bench validation, frequency response plots, sensitivity and stability metrics, a comparison with published methods, and an endurance study to quantify drift and failure modes.

content.text: COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 was used with the Piezoelectric Devices interface. The mesh used tetrahedral elements with maximum element size 0.3 mm on taxel faces and graded coarser regions away from the array. Harmonic sweeps were performed from 1 Hz to 200 Hz with 0.5 Hz resolution near expected resonances and 2 Hz resolution elsewhere. On the bench, a calibrated linear actuator applied sinusoidal forces with amplitude ranges 0.1–50 N and frequencies 1–200 Hz. Force measurement used a calibrated load cell (S-Beam, 100 N range, accuracy 0.2%). Environmental control kept temperature at $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and relative humidity at 45% RH. Acquisition parameters: ADC 24-bit, per-channel sampling $f_s=5\ \mathrm{kHz}$ during validation, anti-aliasing filter corner at 1 kHz, and shielding to reduce mains pickup. For endurance testing, a pneumatic actuator cycled the contact at 2 Hz for 10,000 cycles while logging peak amplitude every 100 cycles.

section4b.title: Frequency Response, Sensitivity and Noise Analysis

content.text: Simulated harmonic sweeps show a dominant resonance near $f_n\approx47\ \mathrm{Hz}$ for each spring-supported taxel, consistent with the lumped estimate in (7). At $F=10\ \mathrm{N}$ and frequency 47 Hz the simulated open-circuit voltage peaks at $V_{\mathrm{peak}}=3.72\ \mathrm{V}$; COMSOL predicted nodal voltages across the electrode consistent with the simplified analytical estimate from (4). Bench measurements returned $V_{\mathrm{peak}}=3.68\ \mathrm{V}$ under nominally identical conditions, indicating a simulation-to-measurement agreement within 1.1% after accounting for adhesive layer compliance and measurement uncertainty. Sensitivity measured as $S=\Delta V/\Delta F$ in the linear region around 1–15 N was $12.4\ \mathrm{mV/N}$. Noise floor measured with shorted inputs was $V_{\mathrm{noise,RMS}}\approx120\ \mu\mathrm{V}$, yielding an SNR of $20\log_{10}(3.72/0.00012)\approx71\ \mathrm{dB}$ at resonance; under normal operating amplitudes SNR remained above 32 dB for $F\geq10\ \mathrm{N}$. Rise time to 90% of steady-state for stepped force inputs averaged 7.6 ms across five trials.

Fig. 7 plots peak voltage versus excitation frequency for selected force amplitudes and overlays simulation and measurement points. The resonance grows slightly with force due to nonlinear contact stiffening from the spring assembly, an effect reproduced in COMSOL when including contact stiffness changes. Off-resonance response follows the analytical scaling predicted by (4) with modest deviations arising from distributed stress fields and fringe electric fields near taxel edges. Crosstalk between adjacent taxels was measured by exciting a single taxel and recording induced voltage on neighbors; typical induced amplitude was 4–6% of the primary taxel under stiff backing and increased to 9–12% with softer backing, indicating a tradeoff between compliance and isolation.

content.text: We compute sensitivity via (5) using linear regression on measured voltage versus applied force in the 1–15 N range. Statistical confidence intervals were obtained using bootstrap resampling (n=1000) yielding a 95% CI of ±0.4 mV/N. Stability metrics were computed from the cycle-resolved peak amplitudes where drift percent is defined as $\mathrm{Drift}(\%)=100\times(V_{\mathrm{initial}}-V_{\mathrm{final}})/V_{\mathrm{initial}}$. For the proposed sensor the measured drift after 10,000 cycles was 4.2%, primarily attributable to minor delamination at the adhesive interface and viscoelastic relaxation of the polymer backing.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compare the proposed PVDF 4×4 taxel array with representative published tactile sensors including ceramic PZT single elements, single-layer PVDF, and capacitive arrays. Table IV summarizes accuracy of touch detection, typical latency, and hardware needs. PZT sensors deliver higher sensitivity per unit area but suffer brittle behavior and require higher voltage poling and complex mounting [19]. Capacitive arrays offer good static pressure sensitivity and low drift but require careful shielding and are sensitive to humidity [20][21]. Single-layer PVDF sensors are simple but show larger crosstalk when used in dense arrays. The proposed approach trades slightly lower per-taxel sensitivity for mechanical compliance, lower weight, and an architecture that achieves low latency (12.3 ms measured round-trip between touch and digital output) suitable for semiconductor handling tasks where soft contact is needed.

An ablation study isolates the effects of spring stiffness, adhesive thickness, and taxel spacing. Reducing spring constant by 50% increases sensitivity by ~18% but increases crosstalk to ~11%. Increasing adhesive thickness from 0.2 mm to 0.6 mm reduces peak voltage by ~9% due to mechanical attenuation. Increasing spacing from 3 mm to 6 mm reduces crosstalk below 2% at the cost of enlarging the sensor footprint. These tradeoffs guide selection depending on application priorities—sensitivity versus spatial resolution.

content.text: Endurance testing cycled a representative taxel under 10 N contact at 2 Hz for 10,000 cycles. Peak voltage was recorded every 100 cycles. Drift was measured at 4.2% relative decrease over the full test. Failure modes observed included minor adhesive delamination at two taxels (12.5% of elements) and a single electrical open due to wire solder fatigue. Thermal stability tests between 10 °C and 40 °C showed voltage variation less than 3% across this range when normalized for force, indicating acceptable thermal tolerance for controlled lab and semiconductor cleanroom environments. The overall reliability is acceptable for prototype tactile arrays but would require improved adhesive selection and strain-relief wiring for production-grade deployment.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This paper presented a combined COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 simulation and bench validation study of a PVDF film piezoelectric tactile sensor arranged as a 4×4 taxel array with 12 mm × 12 mm taxels, 3 mm spacing, and 6 mm total thickness producing an approximately 50 mm × 50 mm sensing area. The electromechanical constitutive framework (strain-charge relations) was implemented in COMSOL with Rayleigh damping and spring supports to represent localized compliance. Analytical expressions such as $V=\dfrac{d_{31}Ft}{\epsilon A}$ and $f_n=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$ provided first-order estimates that matched COMSOL harmonic analysis and bench results.

Key quantitative outcomes include peak voltage $V_{\mathrm{peak}}=3.72\ \mathrm{V}$ at $F=10\ \mathrm{N}$ and $f\approx47\ \mathrm{Hz}$, sensitivity $S=12.4\ \mathrm{mV/N}$ measured in the linear operating range, SNR above 32 dB in typical operating conditions, rise time below 8 ms, and endurance drift of 4.2% after 10,000 cycles. The proposed sensor compared favorably in latency and integration simplicity versus PZT and capacitive alternatives while maintaining reasonable sensitivity for tactile tasks.

There remain limitations and opportunities for future work. Adhesive delamination and wire fatigue observed in endurance tests suggest the need for optimized packaging, strain relief, and alternative adhesive materials tailored for polymer-metal interfaces. The present COMSOL model uses Rayleigh damping as an approximation for viscoelastic losses; a more detailed viscoelastic constitutive model calibrated to dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) data would improve predictive fidelity for long-term behavior. Future work will also explore multi-layer PVDF architectures, improved electrode patterning to reduce fringe fields, and ASIC-level readout that minimizes input capacitance and further reduces noise. We plan to integrate the sensor into a semiconductor wafer-handling gripper and evaluate performance in a cleanroom environment with real wafer contacts.
